findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `HEAD; some-command` or `$(some-command)`, `exec` runs additional commands with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` safely passed the value as one Git argument.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve ownership of the Git process for cancellation
findings.body: `exec` returns the shell process instead of reliably giving callers direct ownership of `git`. Killing the returned child during a slow operation can leave Git running and holding CPU, I/O, or pipes. Using `execFile` keeps cancellation attached to the Git process.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve the Git process as the returned child
findings.body:
On POSIX, a valid Git branch ending in `&` (for example, `feature&`) produces `git show feature&`, which backgrounds Git. The returned shell can emit `exit` while Git is still running, and subsequent `kill()` calls cannot cancel Git, causing premature state transitions and orphaned work.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of a shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. Any caller-controlled value such as `main; rm -rf ...` or `$(command)` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges; the previous `execFile` implementation passed it safely as one argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so any untrusted branch value can execute arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. On POSIX, `showBranch("HEAD; touch /tmp/pwned")` runs `touch`; the previous `execFile` implementation treated the entire value as a Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct ownership of the Git process for cancellation
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than `git` itself. On systems where the shell forks `git`, calling `.kill()` on the returned `ChildProcess`—for example after a timeout during a large or slow `git show`—can leave `git` running and holding its I/O pipes. Repeated cancellations can accumulate orphaned CPU/I/O work and prevent timely cleanup. `execFile()` allowed callers to terminate `git` directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
